channel.title: Signal Brief · Industry
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: Atom Computing finalises $100 million Commerce Department award
item.description: Atom Computing has signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the US Department of Commerce to accelerate research and development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers built on neutral atoms. The award, made under the CHIPS and Science Act, follows a letter of intent announced earlier in 2026 and will fund in-house technology work, expanded engineering and testing infrastructure, and supply chain collaboration. Atom also recently advanced to Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, with potential funding of up to $300 million. Why it matters for tech: Federal funding at this scale signals that neutral-atom quantum computing is now treated as strategic infrastructure, not just research.

item.title: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigns; finance chief Colette Kress takes over on an interim basis
item.description: Nvidia has announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of the board, effective immediately, ending 33 years as chief executive of the company he co-founded in 1993. The announcement gave no reason for the departure, which followed days of reports about Huang's personal conduct and a board investigation, while chief financial officer Colette Kress takes over as interim chief executive and the board searches for a permanent successor. The board also named longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, and Nvidia confirmed its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results will still be reported on November 17 as scheduled. Why it matters for tech: A change at the top of the chipmaker at the centre of the AI buildout will shape chip supply, pricing and US export policy debates.

item.title: Q-CTRL raises $290 million and becomes the quantum sector's newest unicorn
item.description: Q-CTRL has raised US$290 million in a Series C round led by Salesforce Ventures, with participation from Bullhound Capital and Affinity Partners, reaching unicorn status. The oversubscribed round was expanded twice to meet investor demand, and the company says it is the largest fundraise for a software-focused quantum business. Q-CTRL plans to use the money to expand globally, strengthen its AI-powered quantum software, and scale customer programs in finance, energy, autonomy and aerospace, including its Ironstone Opal navigation system that works without GPS. Why it matters for tech: Private money is concentrating on the software layer that makes quantum hardware usable, and a round of this size signals where investors expect value to sit.

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide
item.description: Microsoft is investigating a widespread Microsoft 365 outage that began on Thursday at 1:26 PM ET and left customers unable to connect to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot and Defender XDR. Microsoft said the disruption was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable, which strained the remaining infrastructure, and it has paused deployments, redistributed traffic and begun restarting servers. By Thursday evening Microsoft reported limited recovery after returning some servers to service, but had not confirmed when services would be fully restored. Why it matters for tech: A single outage that takes out mail, chat and AI assistance at once shows how much daily work now depends on one provider's infrastructure.

item.title: TSMC plans $1 billion in stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic
item.description: TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI, with its board approving the plans. Up to $500 million would go into OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors, and $500 million into Anthropic common shares at the price of its expected public listing. TSMC manufactures most of NVIDIA's AI data-centre chips and most of Apple's custom chips, while Anthropic and OpenAI buy large volumes of TSMC-made hardware for their data-centre projects. Why it matters for tech: A chipmaker taking stakes in the AI developers that buy its hardware ties supplier and buyer together, and analysts warn this kind of circular financing makes real demand for AI hardware harder to read.

item.title: More than 20,000 veterans have claimed a free year of ChatGPT Plus
item.description: OpenAI says more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans claimed a year of ChatGPT Plus at no cost in the past year. OpenAI Academy and community partners have hosted more than a dozen training sessions for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, with seven more scheduled before the year ends. The post marks Veterans Day and describes veterans using ChatGPT to organise job searches, rehearse for interviews and turn military experience into civilian resumes. Why it matters for tech: The milestone shows AI training reaching veterans as a career-transition tool, not just a workplace product, and the free access is tied to hands-on teaching rather than a bare giveaway.

item.title: SoftBank sells its entire Nvidia stake for $5.83 billion to fund its AI push
item.description: SoftBank has confirmed it sold all 32.1 million Nvidia shares it held, for $5.83 billion, during October, as it reported second-quarter results on November 10. Chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto said the sale was a financing measure to fund SoftBank's AI investments, including the Stargate data-centre project and its investment in OpenAI. SoftBank also reported second-quarter net profit of 2.5 trillion yen, more than double a year earlier and far above analyst forecasts, helped by gains in its Vision Fund. Why it matters for tech: Selling out of Nvidia to pay for data centres and an OpenAI stake shows the scale of cash SoftBank is moving to fund its AI plans, and the sale weighed on Nvidia's share price.

item.title: D-Wave revenue rises 21% as bookings and contracted revenue climb
item.description: D-Wave reported third-quarter revenue of $4.5 million, up 21% from a year earlier, with nine-month bookings of $37.4 million, up 611%, and contracted revenue still to be recognised of $38.3 million. The company signed a definitive agreement with the US Department of Commerce giving it access to up to $100 million in CHIPS and Science Act funding, in instalments tied to milestones, to develop larger annealing and gate-model machines. NTT DOCOMO deployed a second production application using D-Wave's hybrid quantum technology for mobile network operations. Why it matters for tech: Rising bookings and a large contracted-revenue balance, alongside federal funding for bigger machines, show a quantum vendor converting pilot deployments into paid production work.

item.title: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on gas turbines to power AI data centres
item.description: Anthropic has agreed to spend $3.4 billion on 1.7 gigawatts of gas-powered generators, taking over Texas supplier OnePWR Solutions' existing Caterpillar orders placed about two years ago. The deal, reached in late September according to Reuters, also covers engineering and construction work. It lets Anthropic sidestep a waitlist for turbines that averages six years in the United States. Why it matters for tech: Securing power generation directly shows that electricity supply, not just chips, now sets the pace for AI data centre expansion, and it ties a leading AI lab to new gas capacity.

item.title: Disney and Adobe agree a multi-year alliance on generative AI tools
item.description: Disney and Adobe have announced a multi-year strategic alliance on generative AI tools. Disney gets early access to Adobe's AI tools and will use Firefly, Photoshop, Express, Premiere Pro and Adobe Experience Manager across its businesses, including Walt Disney Imagineering, its resorts and cruise line, and ESPN graphics. The two companies will also develop new generative AI tools together for Disney's franchises. Why it matters for tech: The deal puts Adobe's tools at the centre of Disney's creative pipeline and gives Adobe a flagship entertainment customer to shape its AI products around.

item.title: Nvidia board opens independent review of chief executive after spy reports
item.description: Nvidia's board of directors said it is opening an independent investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who US officials believe was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang supports the review and will cooperate. The New York Times reported last month on the relationship, which Huang later described as romantic in a memo to staff. Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer, is under a Commerce Department investigation into alleged smuggling of AI chips to China. Why it matters for tech: The review sits where chip export controls meet corporate governance, and its outcome shapes how Nvidia handles foreign-intelligence risk at the top of the company.

item.title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue Suno over AI music clones
item.description: Rights holders for Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records have sued AI music company Suno, saying it generates music and lyrics that mimic the artists. The Presley suit says Suno violated Tennessee's ELVIS Act, which bars AI companies from cloning a singer's voice. Suno says it prohibits unauthorised use of an artist's work, blocks prompts naming specific artists, and screens uploads for misuse. The suits follow similar claims by Jason Isbell and others in September and add to cases already brought by Sony and Universal Music Group. Why it matters for tech: The cases test whether voice and likeness laws cover AI-generated imitations, a question that decides how music AI tools can be built and sold.

item.title: IonQ posts record $173.8 million quarter and raises full-year guidance
item.description: IonQ reported record third-quarter revenue of $173.8 million, up 336% year over year, its sixth consecutive record quarter. The company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $505 million and $515 million, from $450 million to $460 million, and said its backlog reached $1.2 billion. Net income was $564.0 million, or $1.42 per share, reflecting a non-cash mark-to-market gain on warrants. Why it matters for tech: Six straight record quarters and a $1.2 billion backlog show demand for quantum systems is outrunning supply.

item.title: Quantinuum revenue up 233% to $9.1 million as it raises its outlook
item.description: Quantinuum reported third-quarter revenue of $9.1 million, up 233% year over year, and raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to between $31 million and $34 million, from $28 million to $32 million. The company also reported a net loss of $118 million and cash of $1.94 billion, and said it signed its largest cloud agreement to date, a multi-year deal with a global financial institution. On hardware, its Helios system reached 99.9995% logical memory fidelity in October, which the company says is within the accuracy range targeted for its Apollo machine. Why it matters for tech: Revenue up 233% with a raised outlook shows trapped-ion systems are converting research progress into paying customers.

item.title: IQM revenue up 51 percent as backlog passes €100 million
item.description: IQM Quantum Computers reported third quarter revenue of €8.86 million, up 50.7 percent on a year earlier, and an order backlog of €102.5 million after booking €42.2 million in new orders during the quarter. The Finnish company reaffirmed full year revenue guidance of €42 million to €47 million and closed its largest contract to date, a €33 million deal with the LUMI AI Factory. It also sold its first system in South America and a second system in Japan. Why it matters for tech: Order books are growing faster than revenue for a quantum hardware maker, which is the clearest signal yet that buyers are committing real money.

item.title: Protesters enter Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
item.description: About 100 protesters entered the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, according to Reuters, in a protest against three 85 metre towers planned for the outskirts of the city. Amsterdam has banned new data centres until 2030, but the project dates to 2016 and proceeds as planned, with Microsoft as sole tenant. It is the latest in a week of actions against data centre building, after voters in the United States rejected data centre development in local ballots earlier in the week. Why it matters for tech: Data centre building is meeting organised local resistance in Europe as well as the US, and older approvals are letting projects proceed despite new bans.

item.title: Horizon Quantum plans to buy error correction specialist Entropica Labs for $27 million
item.description: Horizon Quantum signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire Singapore based quantum software company Entropica Labs for about $27 million in Horizon Quantum Class A ordinary shares. Entropica Labs specialises in error correction and fault tolerance. The deal still needs due diligence, audits and definitive agreements. Why it matters for tech: Quantum software firms are consolidating around error correction, the capability every hardware maker needs before fault tolerant machines arrive.

item.title: Agility Robotics lists on Nasdaq as humanoid robots face scrutiny over scale
item.description: Agility Robotics, maker of the Digit humanoid robot, listed on the Nasdaq on November 5 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, becoming the first dedicated humanoid robot developer to trade publicly in the US. Digit robots already work at customer sites including GXO warehouses and a Schaeffler factory, and the next model, Digit 5, arrives in 2027 with 50 pound lifting and more than 20 hours of work per day. The company's filing shows $1.8 million of revenue in 2025 against a $140 million operating loss, and notes humanoid robots remain unproven at scale. Why it matters for tech: A public listing tests whether investors will fund humanoid robots before the market proves itself, and Agility's numbers show how early that bet still is.

item.title: IonQ completes $1.15 billion acquisition of security firm Elisity
item.description: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a zero trust security company, in an all stock transaction. IonQ's own announcement says it issued 1.15 billion US dollars of consideration in common stock at closing, with up to 150 million dollars more payable if Elisity meets revenue milestones through January 2028, and that Elisity's technology complements its post quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution work. Why it matters for tech: A quantum computing company is adding an operating security business to its revenue base.

item.title: Quint Computing raises €9.1 million seed round for hardware level quantum error correction
item.description: Quint Computing has secured €9.1 million (10.2 million US dollars) in seed funding plus a €2.2 million European Innovation Council Pathfinder grant. The company says its architecture aims to reduce physical error correction overhead by up to 100 times, using continuous electrical control in superconducting circuits. Why it matters for tech: Error correction is where quantum hardware economics are decided, and investors are funding it at the hardware layer.

item.title: Apple home robot reported for 2027 at around $1,000
item.description: Ars Technica reports that Apple is preparing a roaming home robot for 2027, priced at about $1,000, with FaceTime and smart home controls among its functions. The device is reported to have backing from CEO John Ternus and a limited initial feature set. Why it matters for tech: It puts Apple into home robotics, a new product category for the company, at a four figure price point.
